title: Data types and safe conversion
goal: Choose a useful data type and identify values that cannot be converted.
prerequisites: You can select a column and create a new column.

cells.title: A number and its text are different
cells.explanation: A data type tells pandas what a column contains and which operations make sense. Quotation marks make "20" text. `astype()` converts values when the requested conversion is possible.
cells.code:
ages = pd.Series(["20", "21", "19"], dtype="string")
result = ages.astype("int64")
print("Before:", ages.dtype)
print("After:", result.dtype)
print("Next year:", (result + 1).tolist())

questions.prompt: What do the quotation marks around the ages tell Python?
questions.answer: These values are strings, even though they contain digits.

questions.prompt: What will the next-year ages be?

questions.answer: We want numeric addition; text values are not numeric ages yet.

cells.task: Start again with the same text ages. Convert them to numbers and calculate their mean in `result`.
cells.hint: Convert the Series first; then call `.mean()`.
cells.solution:
ages = pd.Series(["20", "21", "19"], dtype="string")
result = ages.astype("int64").mean()
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The mean is 20.0. The conversion makes arithmetic meaningful.

check.prompt: Which expression requests a numeric type?
check.feedback: int64 is an integer data type; string is text.

cells.watch: Do not assume a column is numeric just because its displayed values look like numbers.

cells.title: Convert messy numbers and keep the reason
cells.explanation: `pd.to_numeric()` parses values as numbers. With `errors="coerce"`, values it cannot parse become missing. Preserve the source so you can distinguish an invalid label from a value that was already missing.
cells.code:
source = pd.Series(["88", "absent", None, "72"], dtype="string")
numbers = pd.to_numeric(source, errors="coerce")
invalid = source.notna() & numbers.isna()
result = pd.DataFrame({"Original": source, "Number": numbers, "Invalid_text": invalid})
print(result)

questions.prompt: What does `errors="coerce"` ask pandas to do?
questions.answer: Replace a value that cannot be parsed as a number with a missing value.

questions.prompt: Which row is marked as invalid text?
questions.answer: Only row 1, containing "absent". Row 2 was already missing.

questions.prompt: Why should we keep the original values?
questions.answer: Conversion alone loses the distinction between invalid text and an originally missing value; "absent" may also have a special policy meaning.

cells.task: Change "absent" to "90" in the source. Rebuild the table and count the missing numbers.
cells.solution:
source = pd.Series(["88", "90", None, "72"], dtype="string")
numbers = pd.to_numeric(source, errors="coerce")
invalid = source.notna() & numbers.isna()
result = pd.DataFrame({"Original": source, "Number": numbers, "Invalid_text": invalid})
print(result)
print("Missing numbers:", numbers.isna().sum())
cells.solution_note: Only the original None remains missing; there are no invalid text values.

check.prompt: Does converting "absent" to a missing value mean the score was zero?
options: Yes, missing and zero are identical
No; a grading rule must determine what absent means
Yes, pandas automatically applies grading rules
check.feedback: Parsing is a technical operation. It does not decide the meaning or grading treatment of absence.

cells.verify:
assert result["Number"].isna().sum() == 2
assert result["Invalid_text"].tolist() == [False, True, False, False]
cells.watch: Do not silently turn every conversion failure into zero.
cells.takeaway: Audit conversion failures before deciding how to handle them.

cells.title: Integers that can be missing
cells.explanation: Pandas nullable integer type `Int64` can store whole numbers and `pd.NA`. Its capital I matters. Comparisons can also be missing, so decide how missing comparisons should behave in a filter.
cells.code:
ages = pd.Series([20, None, 22], dtype="Int64")
result = ages + 1
print(result)
print("Known ages:", ages.notna().sum())

questions.prompt: What does the capital I in `Int64` select?
questions.answer: Pandas nullable integer type, which supports a missing-value marker.

questions.prompt: What happens to the missing age when 1 is added?
questions.answer: It remains missing; pandas does not invent an age.

questions.prompt: Why is None not an age of zero?
questions.answer: It means the age was not recorded, while zero would be an actual number.

cells.task: Start with the same ages and keep only known ages of at least 21. Store the filtered Series in `result`.
cells.solution:
ages = pd.Series([20, None, 22], dtype="Int64")
mask = (ages >= 21).fillna(False)
result = ages[mask]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Only 22 remains. The explicit False says an unknown age does not satisfy this selection rule.

check.prompt: Which value remains missing after adding 1?

cells.verify:
assert result.iloc[0] == 21
assert pd.isna(result.iloc[1])
assert result.iloc[2] == 23
cells.watch: Do not write `if pd.NA:`; its truth value is ambiguous. Use `.isna()` or `.notna()`.
cells.takeaway: Use nullable types when missing values are legitimate.

cells.title: Categories and an explicit order
cells.explanation: A category stores values drawn from a defined set, such as programs or rating bands. An ordered category has a meaningful sequence that you choose. Sorting follows that sequence instead of alphabetical order.
cells.code:
ratings = pd.Series(["High", "Low", "Medium", "Low"], dtype="string")
rating_type = pd.CategoricalDtype(["Low", "Medium", "High"], ordered=True)
result = ratings.astype(rating_type).sort_values()
print(result)
print("Order:", result.cat.categories.tolist())

questions.prompt: Where is the rating order defined?
Which value appears first after sorting?
questions.answer: Low, followed by the other Low, then Medium and High.

questions.prompt: Why might alphabetical sorting be wrong here?
questions.answer: Alphabetical sorting puts High first, which does not represent the intended rating order.

cells.task: Use students(). Make Program an ordered category with IT before AI, then sort by Program and Student_ID. Store the sorted Student_ID and Program columns in the DataFrame result.
cells.solution:
df = students()
program_type = pd.CategoricalDtype(["IT", "AI"], ordered=True)
df["Program"] = df["Program"].astype(program_type)
result = df.sort_values(["Program", "Student_ID"])[["Student_ID", "Program"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: All six IT students appear before the six AI students; each program is ordered by ID.

check.feedback: The category sequence becomes the ordering used by sorting and comparisons.

cells.watch: A value outside a declared category list becomes missing when converted; check the result.
cells.takeaway: Define category meaning and order deliberately.
